copies.headline: Loaded at the skill spots, thin at running back
copies.body:
Adam built this the way he builds everything — steady, top-heavy where it counts, and light on panic. Jaxon Smith-Njigba at 7 was already good value, and Chris Olave falling to round 3 gave him a top-ten receiver on top of it. Rome Odunze in round 5 is a bet on name recognition more than current cost, but the WR room carries this team either way. The real coup came in round 7, where Jayden Daniels sitting at pick 79 is the single best value anybody drafted this year — a QB5 talent for QB-nobody-cared price, backed up by Brock Purdy a round later at another absurd discount. Sam LaPorta in round 6 is the one swing that missed, a full round early for a TE8.
Running back is the soft spot. Kenneth Walker was a reach at 18, Bucky Irving and Brian Robinson cost more than late-RB rooms usually justify, and depth behind them is Rico Dowdle and Kenny Gainwell — capable, unspectacular, one injury from ugly. Still, the top of this roster is a real problem for the league, and Adam knows it. He's 34-22 for a reason. He just needs Isaac to stop being the one guy who has his number.

copies.headline: Loaded on top, empty in the middle
copies.body:
Peter built this the way you'd build a team if you'd already decided the RB position was a lost cause and refused to pay retail anywhere else. Bijan Robinson at 1.2 is the RB2 off the board and fine, if unspectacular, as a floor. Everything after him is the story: A.J. Brown at 23 and Tee Higgins at 47 are legitimate values, George Pickens gives him a third alpha receiver, and Lamar Jackson falling to round 5 is the best pick anyone made on this roster — a QB2-caliber arm at QB9 pricing. Dak Prescott as insurance in round 13 at plus-30 value is almost unfair. That's an A-grade WR room and an A-grade QB room stacked on the same team.
The cost is the running back depth, which is a graveyard after Bijan — Jonathon Brooks, Jordan Mason, Kyle Monangai, Chris Rodriguez all cratered relative to cost, with Mason standing as the actual biggest reach in the entire draft. Tucker Kraft was paid for a touch early too. One Bijan injury and this offense is throwing on every down, which, given the receivers, might not be the worst plan. Still trailing John 3-6, still chasing 2022. This is the closest he's come back.

copies.headline: Loaded receiver room, running back mess
copies.body:
The Aura Farm built this around CeeDee Lamb and DeVonta Smith, and that duo alone makes the WR room the best on the roster by a wide margin — Lamb still a top-five option even at a slightly rich price, Smith a legitimate value at pick 38. Jameson Williams and Khalil Shakir add ceiling depth behind them. The problem is everything drafted at running back before the double-digit rounds: Chase Brown and Travis Etienne both cost more than their current standing supports, Bhayshul Tuten and Aaron Jones are complementary pieces being asked to be answers. George Kittle at TE was an overpay, and Deebo Samuel in round 9 is Christian's worst pick by a mile, a 56th-ranked receiver taken like a top-40 one. The saving grace is the quarterback room — Trevor Lawrence as a value pickup, then Jordan Love falling to round 14 was his best pick of the draft, pure profit at the position.
Christian's whole deal is boom-or-bust, 10-4 one year and 4-10 the next, and this roster reads exactly like that: an elite top end at receiver carrying a shaky running back corps that could sink him again.

copies.headline: Backfield Loaded, Receivers an Afterthought
copies.body:
Noah built this one from the ground up, and it shows. Cook and Achane give him two RB1-caliber engines, with Achane at #17 the clear steal of his draft. Rhamondre Stevenson adds cheap thump behind them in round 7. Then in round 5 he got Drake Maye at QB3 value, his best pick by a mile — a top-12 arm at a QB2's price. Colston Loveland gives him a real receiving threat at tight end, rounding out a room graded A across QB, RB, and TE.
The wheels come off at wide receiver. Garrett Wilson and Mike Evans were both taken ahead of their market, and the bottom of the roster is a graveyard of dart throws — Josh Downs at pick 89 is his worst pick, and Romeo Doubs and Jordyn Tyson didn't do him any favors either. It's a WR2 problem hiding behind an elite core, which tracks for a guy whose title came from the 7 seed nobody trusted in round one either.

copies.headline: Top-heavy stars, empty tight end room
copies.body:
Logan built this the only way that makes sense in a league where he's cursed at the top of the standings: pay for stars and worry about depth later. Justin Jefferson anchors the receiving corps, and pairing him with Jalen Hurts — a sixth-round QB who plays for the team Saquon Barkley now runs behind — gives this roster real top-end thump. Barkley came at pick 15, pricier than his current RB8 slot, but Jeremiyah Love at 34 was his best value, a third-round flier on a back who profiles as a bigger name than his RB15 cost. Tetairoa McMillan and Luther Burden add rookie upside behind Jefferson, though both went a round early.
The cracks show late. Isaiah Likely at TE was his worst pick, a ninth-round reach for a room ESPN grades a D outright, and the RB and WR benches thin out fast into replacement-level names like Dobbins and Allgeier. Still, A-grade QB and WR rooms carry this. Logan's owned back-to-back top seeds and zero playoff wins — the stars are here again, the depth is the same old excuse waiting to happen.

copies.headline: Loaded skill spots, paid over sticker
copies.body:
Jeanty and Breece Hall give Kaleb two true bell-cow backs, though Jeanty at 12 overall was a reach and Hall in round three was the sharper of the two buys. The receiver room is where the ceiling lives — Drake London and Ladd McConkey are legit WR1/2 material even if both cost more than consensus said they should, and Harold Fannin Jr. gives him a top-five TE, albeit at a sixth-round price nobody else was paying. Then it gets messy: Carnell Tate, Jordan Addison, KC Concepcion, Kenyon Sadiq, Keenan Allen and Tre Tucker were all bought well above market, six swings in a row that missed on value even if a couple stick as depth. Justin Herbert in round eight is his best pick of the draft, and Jared Goff even later gives him a real QB2 for nothing.
This is a talented, top-heavy roster built by a guy allergic to letting anyone else get a player he wanted — which tracks for a franchise stuck on three straight 8-6 finishes since that 2023 title. The name still says Cinderella. The recent résumé says pumpkin.

copies.headline: Loaded Backfield, Cloudy Everywhere Else
copies.body:
Jonathan Taylor at 1.09 is the anchor here, a legitimate RB4 who anchors the whole build, and CJ backed him up by hoarding running backs like it's 2019 — Judkins, Henderson, Hubbard, Pacheco, Charbonnet all landed between rounds 3 and 12. Some of that is organizational depth insurance, but Judkins at #33 and Pacheco in round 11 were both significant reaches, and that's a lot of capital on bodies who won't touch a starting snap. The receiving corps is thinner than the RB room suggests it should be — Rashee Rice and Emeka Egbuka are quality WR2/3 types but both cost more than their rank, and Parker Washington and Alec Pierce round out a room that lacks a true alpha. Jake Ferguson at TE is replacement-level at best.
Where this draft gets interesting is the quarterback room: Joe Burrow in round 6 is the clear steal, and Tyler Shough as a round-14 dart throw is absurd value on paper. CJ built an A-grade QB room almost by accident while overspending everywhere else. For a guy still chasing his only winning season, that Burrow pick might be the one that finally tips the seed his way — Leif's 4-4 rivalry included.

copies.headline: Elite tight ends, shaky running back room
copies.body:
John built this thing top-down and it shows. Puka Nacua at 1.04 was pricey but he's a legitimate WR2 anchor, and pairing him with Brock Bowers and Trey McBride gives this roster the best tight end room in the league by a mile — McBride at pick 28 was value, getting a top-two TE that late. Kyren Williams in round four is his best pick of the draft, a workhorse back at a discount. But the RB room falls apart after him: D'Andre Swift was a reach, and by rounds 9 through 12 he was throwing darts at Blake Corum, Tyrone Tracy Jr. and Keaton Mitchell, none of which landed. Quentin Johnston in round eight is his worst pick, and Brian Thomas Jr. two rounds earlier wasn't much better. Stafford at 148 as insurance for Caleb Williams, though, was outright theft.
The older Lundquist brother leads Peter 6-3 all-time and still hasn't found a roster that finishes the job. This one's got a ceiling if the backfield holds together — it probably won't.

copies.headline: Loaded at Two Spots, Thin Everywhere Else
copies.body:
Mitchell built this thing top-down and never really stopped paying retail. Jahmyr Gibbs at 1.01 is a legitimate workhorse anchor, and pairing him with Josh Jacobs gives the RB room real floor even if Jacobs at #25 cost more than his current RB18 profile says he's worth. Nico Collins is a fine WR2-caliber piece up top, but after him the receiver room turns into a pile of late-round hope — DJ Moore, Courtland Sutton, Matthew Golden and Tank Dell were all taken well ahead of where the market had them, and Golden in particular was a bad round-8 swing. Tight end is the one room that's genuinely stacked: Tyler Warren gives him a rookie with TE1 upside, and grabbing Travis Kelce in round 10 was the shrewdest thing he did all draft. Quarterback is Jaxson Dart and Daniel Jones, which is a bye-week fill-in plan more than a QB room.
Alvin Kamara in round 16 was pure profit, but one late steal doesn't offset a draft where almost every pick before round 10 came in above market. Mitchell's whole football personality is right there in the record book — three straight 7-7 seasons, somehow two playoff wins anyway. This roster reads the same way: never bad enough to embarrass him, never sharp enough to separate.

copies.headline: Loaded at Receiver, Empty at Quarterback
copies.body:
Isaac built this the way you'd expect from a guy chasing his 2022 high: swing big on the top of the roster and worry about the rest later. Chase at 3 anchors a receiver room that grades out as A-level, and Malik Nabers at 27 is close to market cost. But the price for stacking Terry McLaurin, DK Metcalf, Wan'Dale Robinson and Jakobi Meyers behind them was reaching on all four, McLaurin at -12, Metcalf at -14, Robinson at -20 as his worst pick of the draft. The backfield is thinner than it looks — Javonte Williams was a -14 reach in round 2, and Cam Skattebo (+2) and Jaylen Warren give it some floor but not a clear lead back. Bo Nix at #118 was his best pick, a QB13 falling to round 10, though the room around him (Malik Willis, mostly punting the position all August) is why QB grades D+.
Tight end is a mixed bag saved by Dalton Kincaid falling to round 12. The overall shape here — stars-and-scrubs at receiver, late-round quarterback dice roll — feels like a man still chasing 11-3.

copies.headline: Two Aces, a Loaded Backfield, No Receivers
copies.body:
Leif built this thing from the top down and forgot the middle exists. McCaffrey at 1.05 is a bit early for a back who missed time last year, but pairing him with Derrick Henry in round two gives this backfield real thump, and David Montgomery adds rushing volume even if he came a round earlier than needed. The QB room is the actual headline: Josh Allen at 29 overall is a legitimate steal, and getting Patrick Mahomes as a QB2 in round 13 is close to free. Kyle Pitts anchors the tight end room fine, even at a reach.
Then the wideouts happen. Davante Adams, Stefon Diggs and Jayden Reed were all taken well above their market, and by the time Woody Marks fell into his lap at -30 value the room was already a mess. WR grades out an F here — no depth, no upside, just aging names and dead rounds. Vintage Joey Lunchbox: loyal to a plan long after it stops working, still 22-34 for his career, still dead even with CJ at 4-4. This roster wins with Allen slinging it and the run game grinding — if the receivers ever show up.

copies.headline: Loaded at Receiver, Held Together by Duct Tape
copies.body:
Grant built this thing top-down and never adjusted the plan. Amon-Ra St. Brown at 1.6 is a slight reach for a true WR1, but the room around him is legitimately stacked — Zay Flowers, Jaylen Waddle, Christian Watson, Chris Godwin all stashed as WR2/3 depth that most rosters would kill for, even if the cost on Flowers and Watson ran well above market. Omarion Hampton at 2.19 is the value anchor at running back, but everything after him — Jadarian Price, Tony Pollard, Jacory Croskey-Merritt, Tank Bigsby — was drafted well ahead of where the league had those guys, capped by Croskey-Merritt at pick 91 going 30 spots early. Dallas Goedert and Juwan Johnson were quietly nice value grabs at tight end, and Baker Mayfield in round 13 is the one pick here that looks like theft. The Kyler Murray reach in round 10 says the quarterback room was an afterthought all along.
Grant is the league's live wire — 3-11, then 9-5, then 5-9, no pattern, no brakes — and this roster reads the same way: a real WR corps carrying a shaky, overpaid backfield and a quarterback situation held up by a round-13 miracle.

intro: Draft season shook out top-heavy this year — Adam somehow finds another gear after already owning the best resume in league history, and the tier right behind him (Peter, Christian, Noah) all left the cabin with rosters that look like they printed money. The middle class is crowded and unspectacular, which usually means somebody's B- team quietly wins the thing while everybody argues about tiebreakers. Running back went in bursts all night, with three different owners reaching in the same six-pick window trying to avoid the cliff everyone saw coming. Bottom third is where it gets grim — Isaac, Leif, and Grant all landed in the same gentleman's-C purgatory, which at Players Weekend just means somebody's picking out a dress in December.
